target_columns.name: product_line
target_columns.transformation: Grouping key, carried through unchanged from the joined policy

target_columns.name: claim_quarter
target_columns.transformation: DATEPART(QUARTER, claims.claim_date), grouping key; integer 1-4 based on calendar quarter

target_columns.name: open_count
target_columns.transformation: COUNT of rows where claims.status = 'Open' via SUM(CASE WHEN ...)

target_columns.name: approved_count
target_columns.transformation: COUNT of rows where claims.status = 'Approved' via SUM(CASE WHEN ...)

target_columns.name: rejected_count
target_columns.transformation: COUNT of rows where claims.status = 'Rejected' via SUM(CASE WHEN ...)

target_columns.name: paid_count
target_columns.transformation: COUNT of rows where claims.status = 'Paid' via SUM(CASE WHEN ...)

target_columns.name: total_claims
target_columns.transformation: COUNT(*) of claims rows per group after join to policies

quirks: SUM(CASE WHEN ...) is a manual pivot of claims.status into fixed columns; any status value outside the four hardcoded literals ('Open','Approved','Rejected','Paid') is silently dropped from the per-status counts but still counted in total_claims, so open_count+approved_count+rejected_count+paid_count may be < total_claims -- must preserve this exact bucket set rather than inferring statuses dynamically
DATEPART(QUARTER, ...) is T-SQL-specific; equivalent in Spark is quarter(claim_date) -- verify both yield 1-4 using the same calendar-quarter definition with no fiscal-year offset

INNER JOIN to policies means any claim with a policy_id not present in policies is silently excluded from all rollups -- a LEFT JOIN would change total_claims, so fan-out/filtering behavior must be preserved exactly

GROUP BY repeats the YEAR()/DATEPART() expressions rather than referencing output aliases (SQL Server doesn't allow grouping by SELECT-list alias) -- purely syntactic, no semantic quirk to preserve beyond matching the same three grouping keys in PySpark

Assumes policy_id join key has a 1:1 (or 1:many from policies to claims) relationship; if a claim's policy_id matches multiple policy rows (duplicate policy_id in policies), this join would fan out and inflate all counts -- confirm policy_id uniqueness in policies before treating row counts as claim counts

status comparisons are presumably case-sensitive/exact-match literals ('Open','Approved','Rejected','Paid') -- any casing/whitespace variants in source data (e.g. 'open', 'OPEN ') would not match and would fall through uncounted into the total_claims-only bucket
